title: Faraz Shafiq - Reimagining Banking in the AI Era

segments.text: FARAZ SHAFIQ: Good afternoon, everyone.
It's an absolute pleasure being here.
My name is Faraz Shafiq.
I lead Products and Solutions for Wells Fargo.
We've largely lived in a world that
has been defined by what we call cognitive scarcity.
So think before AI.
Even though it's very hard to think before AI.
But think before November 2022.
If you needed to build a mobile app, you needed to hire people,
hire organizations that had the special skill set
to build a mobile app.
Just like that.
Before, you needed to build a website,
you needed specialized skills, specialized teams
to build a website.
What's different about AI is that we are now in the world
defined by cognitive abundance, where intelligence is not
the issue anymore.
You want to build a mobile app.
It's as easy as going on Claude or ChatGPT or tens
of others' applications and literally describing
what you want.
And so we believe that we've really
entered into this very new paradigm and a very
new, interesting era.
Now, banking has been around for a long time.
It's hundreds of years old.
But the first time we actually saw physical ATMs come
into the picture in the US was roughly 1960s.
So that's the first time you actually
saw physical ATMs come in.
And so you could actually now go into an ATM,
not go into the bank, but actually just go to the ATM
if you just wanted cash.
Then about 1980s is when telephony started to come in.
And if you could make a simple change via the phone,
you would just call in like, I want to update my address.
I want to do some balance transfer
or just know where is the status of the credit card
that was shipped.
So what happened is, now, people started
using phones for the use cases where phone was a good use case.
And then 2000s with the internet era,
we saw big emergence where people started using the web.
So now you open your laptop, you log in.
You can take a look into your account,
and you can do many, many things on the web.
And then eventually, 2010s, thanks to the iPhone and App
Store.
And I guarantee everyone in this room has at least 1 banking app,
if not 10.
And so every time there was a transition,
there was a big shift.
In the 1960s, ATMs was the only choice.
100% people would go to the ATM or the bank.
When telephone came in, some people would
start going on that route, use the phone,
others would still continue to go to an ATM or bank.
Same with web, the stuff that you can do online,
you'll do online.
The stuff that you-- you have to go to a bank, you would go in.
And so we believe that this year has
been the beginning of another era,
where the interface is being redesigned and refined.
And we believe that the banking experience is actually going
to start within the agent.
And so now, it's about people asking,
going on Claude or ChatGPT and asking,
what should I do about my 529 college plan?
Or, hey, I just have this new job.
It's asking me to relocate to a certain place.
What would be the best way to do that?
And so we're seeing this massive shift where
the information or the intelligence,
and specifically, the user interface
is actually becoming the agent.
To effect where we potentially believe that the future,
you may not need an app anymore because you have an agent that
takes care of that.
And so we do believe that this is the start of a massive
and a new era in the world of AI.
And again, it's not just a demo or a proof point,
but it is an actual working use case.
So for Wells Fargo, our AI assistant just crossed 1 billion
plus customer interactions.
We have 33 million plus active users on the platform.
And we see that wherever these tools are
being used by our customers, by our bankers, we saw roughly 25%
higher increase in both the account openings for deposits
as well as credit cards.
So the amount of time that bankers
spend on drafting notes or looking or researching
into client relationships, most of that
now becomes table stakes.
In fact, it just takes a few minutes and gets that done.
And so again, when we say that agents become the new interface,
again, it's not just hypothetical.
It, in fact, has already begun.
But one thing that always challenges me,
and the more I think about this industry,
is there's a very small group of companies and organizations
that take majority of the value created by AI.
So I'm sure many people here would
resonate with these numbers.
There's tons of tons of studies that 10% of the projects
are the ones that are successful,
or 95% of the projects continue to fail.
So we believe that this is going to continue
to be true for at least the next couple of years.
And the gap is not the model.
And I know there's been a lot of conversations on models,
and the models are unbelievably powerful.
But the model that we're going to use
versus other banks or your organizations
are the same model.
We all have access to Opus 5.0, or Fable, or GPT 5.5.
Our model is not any different than the models
that you all will have access to.
So the differentiator is actually not the model.
The differentiator is the stuff around the model.
How will we use it?
Where will we use it?
The how really depends on things like agentic harnesses, data,
security profile.
Agents are great, but when you get
them doing a long running tasks, they actually
are not that great.
So that's a problem.
If there's entrepreneurs in the room, please look into that.
That's a huge area.
But the big thing is going to be also the culture.
Also, how do you prioritize the right use cases?
Because one thing I see all the time is suddenly
everything becomes AI.
It doesn't matter what you're doing.
And that's not the right approach.
And so for us, it's a matter of taking a very
phased and systematic approach.
Wells Fargo is a 174-year-old company,
and we want to be very meaningful in how we proceed
ahead with AI.
So our approach in the short-term
is to look at AI as a tool, just like you
have your Excel and Word docs and many other tools.
So humans use AI as a tool largely focused
on individual use cases.
So again, you open ChatGPT, you're
the one putting in the prompt, getting that information,
and then using that information to do something.
Then, we believe, very quickly, the world
will move into what we're calling AI as a teammate.
So now it's less about individual productivity.
It's more about system workflows.
The best example I use is, imagine AI
being like a junior employee.
Just like when you hire someone new into the organization,
you need to give them data.
You need to help ramp them up, give them access to systems.
AI would be exactly the same way.
You onboard AI.
You give it the right context.
You give it the information.
And more importantly, you give it
feedback on what is the right way to do things.
So we believe that starting next year, for us,
our focus will go from AI as a tool to AI as a teammate.
That means, when I think about, for example, home lending
or a mortgage process, which is a very complex process, very
human-driven, a lot of manual tasks.
Now, AI is a teammate means when someone comes in and submits
their mortgage application, the person can literally just
trigger an AI agent, and that AI agent automatically
could basically start looking at underwriting,
look at what's needed, things like income
tax and many other things.
And so AI becomes integrated into the workflow.
It's not sitting somewhere else.
It is not limited to one person.
It is part of the team.
In fact, I believe very quickly we're going
to have AI in the org chart.
So we're going to have home mortgage, the leadership team,
then the product management.
And in every area, you're going to have
an AI agent or multiple agents sitting within that.
But the end goal really for us is autonomous AI.
So in the first two cases, it's largely still driven by humans.
Humans are the ones who are prompting it.
Humans are the one who are defining
when it should be triggered.
In autonomous AI, that is when AI will be telling us what to do
and when to do it.
And again, the best example is, just
like you have a junior employee, imagine
you have a senior employee that has access
to the entire customer database, entirety of the internet
is very well versed in your organization, in your processes.
They will be more consistent, more reliable, and largely more
accurate than humans as well.
Even for humans, by the way, the success rate that we've seen
With consistent processes, this can easily beat that.
And so in the world of autonomous AI,
you're not waiting for a trigger,
like someone came in and opened a mortgage application.
The AI could literally be sending you a Slack message
saying, hey, Faraz, I saw that the market rate now
is reduced by the feds.
Should we create a new offering targeted
for certain demographic?
And my job would ideally be just to say yes.
Or better yet, it tells me that, hey,
the market rate actually dropped.
I already did the change because I was 99.7% confident.
I have rolled it out, and these are the new things
that are already happening.
That is the world of autonomous AI.
And again, my personal belief is that 2028 onwards
will be defined by this era.
This doesn't mean we're taking a sequential approach.
Even today, we are experimenting with autonomous AI.
But that just means the mix of things
will really start switching, and that's
where our focus is going to be.
And so for us, we want to change fundamentally
how our bank will operate.
In this era of AI, we're looking at four core pillars.
And those are our core strategy for us.
One is the hub-and-spoke model, which
simply means that there is not going to be a central team.
The job of the AI organization, or an AI team,
or the chief officer is to now enable
everyone else in the organization
not to be the lone builder.
That's what the hub-and-spoke models means, that you
have to give the tools.
You have to have the partnerships, the strategy.
But the execution should sit within the lines of businesses.
For anyone who's a CIO or has worked as an IT person, the word
shadow IT is very scary.
People get very worried about shadow IT,
but there will not be shadow AI.
Because AI will be for everyone and will be used by everyone,
technical or non-technical.
The second thing is to focus on very clear value-driven use
cases.
Not all use cases are equal, and the high-impact use cases
will really drive tremendous value.
The third thing is moving fast.
So we are still a bank.
We're still extremely regulated.
So we want to be very safe, very secure.
We want to take the right level of risks.
And so having those protections is absolutely critical.
So we want to move fast but with a very disciplined approach.
And the final thing is that to really drive value at scale,
we need our people to be upskilled and enabled.
You have to drive adoption.
But remember, adoption does not mean impact.
But for impact at scale, you do need adoption.
And so we really want to drive adoption and impact at scale
and upskill our workforce.
And so for the question for us that
defines our strategy is not what barriers
do we have in technology.
In fact, we talk about technology
very little because technology is changing a lot.
But our business processes, our challenges and opportunities,
those are the real questions.
It doesn't matter where technology
comes in two months from now or three months from now,
the questions we're asking, can we do something better
for our customers?
Those questions still remain the same.
And so for us, every day, we're challenging.
If technology is not the barrier, what will we build?
Thank you.
